claims.text: A two-step heat treatment can induce a controlled dispersion of coherent nanoscale precipitates in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The coherent nanoscale precipitates increase yield strength.
The precipitation treatment retains or enhances ductility relative to the as-cast condition.
The as-cast refractory high-entropy alloy has a relatively homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
Controlled aging after solutionizing precipitates coherent nanoscale particles.
An inert atmosphere is required to avoid oxidation during the treatment.
The treatment requires temperature ranges suitable for first dissolving and then reprecipitating a secondary phase.
The treatment forms uniformly distributed, coherent nanoscale precipitates within the matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitates obstruct dislocation motion and thereby enhance strength.
Coherent precipitate interfaces permit dislocation absorption and multiplication.
Dislocation absorption and multiplication at coherent interfaces prevents the precipitates from becoming weak points that compromise ductility.
The heat-treated alloy will have a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the as-cast alloy.
The heat-treated alloy will maintain or increase ductility relative to the as-cast alloy.
The strength and ductility improvements will be moderate but meaningful for structural applications.
The beneficial effect occurs only when temperature, time, and cooling rate are optimized to form coherent precipitates.
Incoherent precipitates or excessive precipitate coarsening may prevent the desired strength–plasticity improvement.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis permits ductility merely to be retained, whereas the falsification rule requires statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and ductility. A result with significantly increased strength and statistically unchanged ductility would satisfy the stated prediction but could be classified as falsifying it under the rule.
